"Vishal, you forgot the shortcut for the pivot table again?"

"Yep. Third time this year, Lokesh."

"Doesn't that annoy you?"

"It used to. I'd think, I'm getting slow. Now I just open my notes file."

"You keep notes on shortcuts?"

"On everything I don't use every day. And on the first Monday of each month I spend twenty minutes going through the ones I'll need soon."

"That sounds like school."

"It sort of is. But the brain isn't a hard drive. It drops what I don't use. That's normal, not failing."

Lokesh laughed. "I thought forgetting meant I was bad at my job."

"Nope. It means you're human. Want my notes template?"

qa.a: On the first Monday of each month, for twenty minutes.

qa.a: Vishal feels relaxed and unbothered now, whereas before Vishal felt annoyed and worried about getting slow.

passage:
When I started as a physiotherapy assistant, I panicked whenever I forgot a technique I'd learnt in training. I'd lie awake thinking I wasn't cut out for the job.

My supervisor Mehak noticed. She said, "You're not supposed to remember everything. Your brain throws out what you don't use. Keep notes, and review."

So I made a small notebook for rare exercises. Every Sunday evening I read through a few pages, just before they'd fully slipped. When I need one at work, I check the notebook before the session, no shame.

Last month a patient needed a shoulder exercise I hadn't done in a year. I checked my notes, did it right, and felt calm about it.

I'm Samir. Forgetting isn't failing. It's just the mind making space.

qa.q: What did Samir make for rare exercises?
qa.a: A small notebook for rare exercises.

qa.q: How did Samir feel before Mehak's advice?
qa.a: Samir felt panicked and anxious, lying awake and doubting being cut out for the job.

qa.q: What routine could someone new at a job copy from Samir?
qa.a: Keep a notebook for things rarely used and read through a few pages each week, checking notes without shame when needed.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt seeing Samir handle the shoulder exercise?
qa.a: Mehak probably felt pleased and proud that the advice helped Samir feel calm and competent.

grounding: A working adult keeps notes, reviews skills at intervals and treats forgetting as ordinary, not a sign of failing.

I told her forgetting what we don't use is normal. I suggested she keep a pocket notebook and review key procedures every few weeks.

Since then, I've noticed her flipping through the notebook during quiet night shifts. Her colleague Payal has started doing the same.

Last week, during a surprise drill, Nikita checked her notes quickly and led the steps without hesitation. Afterwards she said, "I still forget things, but now it doesn't scare me." I'm suggesting the notebook system to the whole ward.

Imran, class eleven, came to see me today. He said he felt tired of everything: tuition, coaching, family expectations. He kept talking about when he was small. "Life was so easy. I just played cricket all day in the lane."

Everything is too much. Physics test Friday, dance practice, and Mom and Dad keep asking about college. I just want to be seven again. Summer holidays at Grandma's, swimming in the lake, no worries at all.

Then I called Francis, my cousin who was there too. I said, "Remember how perfect those summers were?"

He said, "You were terrified of the lake. You wouldn't go past your knees. And you cried when Grandma made you eat okra."

I laughed so hard. I totally forgot.

Maybe the past wasn't perfect. Maybe I just miss feeling safe. Tomorrow I'll tell Mom I'm stressed instead of pretending I'm fine.

— Ankita

Manoj, you get annoyed when your Nana talks about the good old days? Let your Sonali aunty tell you about my Dadaji.

When I was twenty-five and working in a Mumbai office, I'd visit him in the village. He would say, "In our time, people were honest, the water was sweet, and children respected elders."

At first I argued. I told him about the droughts he himself had described, the debts, the sickness. He'd go silent and stare at the fields.

Then one evening I just listened. I asked about his mother's cooking, his first bicycle. He talked till dark, laughing. I understood the memories were his treasure, even if those years were rougher than he admitted.

He died two years later. I'm so glad I listened more than I argued.

qa.a: She felt a new tenderness, understanding the memories were his treasure even if those years were rougher than he admitted.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to listen kindly to her grandfather's golden memories without arguing, keeping their bond strong.

She'd been feeling this way for a while. She kept remembering the bad times: the dance performance where she tripped, the friend who stopped calling. It felt like facts, not feelings.

Her uncle Zubin, visiting for the week, knocked on her door. "You've been quiet for days. Can I sit?"

Hafsa shrugged. He sat and waited. Slowly she told him.

"That sounds really heavy," he said. "Feeling low for this long isn't something you should carry alone. Let's tell your mum tonight, and find someone good you can talk to." Hafsa nodded, eyes wet.

qa.q: Who knocked on Hafsa's door?
qa.a: Her uncle Zubin, visiting for the week.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa read the silence in the class group as "nobody cares"?
qa.a: Her long low mood made neutral silence feel like rejection and pulled up memories of failures, which felt like facts.

qa.q: What did Zubin do that was helpful?
qa.a: He sat and listened, took her feelings seriously, and planned to tell her mum that night and find a professional to talk to.

qa.q: How might Hafsa's classmates see the unanswered message?
qa.a: They may not have noticed it or were busy, not meaning any rejection at all.

grounding: A teenager in a low mood reads neutral silence as rejection and recalls only failures; a caring adult steps in.

"Kashish, you haven't eaten dinner with us all week."

"Not hungry, Papa."

"Raghav told me you left the cricket group."

"They don't want me. Nobody ever replies to me."

"Raghav said they asked where you were."

"He's just saying that."

"Beta, you've been this low for a while now. Everything looks dark when you feel this way. It doesn't mean it's true."

"It feels true."

"I know. That's why I'm worried. I've booked a time with Dr Mehta for Saturday. I'll come with you. And tonight, can we just sit together?"

Kashish looked at the floor for a long time. "Okay."

qa.q: When did Papa book a time with Dr Mehta?
qa.a: For Saturday.

qa.q: Why does Kashish think the cricket group doesn't want her?
qa.a: Her low mood makes neutral things feel like rejection, so even Raghav's news seems false to her.

qa.q: What did Papa do well?
qa.a: He named the low mood kindly, didn't argue about facts, booked a professional appointment and offered to stay with Kashish that night.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel if he heard Kashish thinks he's just saying things?
qa.a: Raghav might feel hurt or worried, since he was trying to reach out.

grounding: A teenager in a low mood reads neutral messages as rejection; a caring parent responds and seeks professional help.

passage:
Jana, twenty, had just passed her driving test in Berlin and got an A on her history paper the same week. She felt unstoppable.

When her friend Layla asked her to help organise a birthday party, she said yes. When her boss asked her to cover two extra shifts, she said yes. When a classmate suggested a road trip that weekend, she said yes to that too.

"You're doing all three?" Layla asked.

"Easy," Jana said, grinning. "I'll make it work."

By Saturday, she was exhausted, late for the party, and cancelled on the road trip at the last minute. Sitting on the tram, she wondered how everything had seemed so easy on Tuesday.

qa.q: What did Jana pass that week?
qa.a: Her driving test.

qa.q: Why did Jana say yes to everything?
qa.a: She felt joyful and unstoppable after her successes, so every plan seemed easy and the risks seemed small.

qa.q: What could Jana do next time she's in a great mood and gets asked for things?
qa.a: She could say "let me check and get back to you" and look at her schedule before agreeing.

qa.q: How might Layla feel when Jana is late for the party?
qa.a: Layla might feel disappointed and a bit frustrated, since Jana had said it would be easy.

grounding: A young adult in a great mood underestimates risks and says yes to too much.

passage:
At the college sports club, Madhav, nineteen, had just won the inter-college badminton final. He was glowing.

The coach, Kishore sir, came over. "Madhav, would you like to lead the junior training on weekends?"

"Yes! Definitely!"

A classmate asked him to join a hackathon. "Sure, count me in!"

Another friend asked about a night trek on the same weekend. "Absolutely!"

That evening, Kishore sir stopped him. "Madhav, you just agreed to three things on the same Saturday."

Madhav blinked. It hadn't seemed like a problem an hour ago. Everything had felt possible.

"When you're this happy, everything looks easy," the coach said. "Sleep on it and tell me tomorrow."

qa.q: What had Madhav just won?
qa.a: The inter-college badminton final.

qa.q: Why didn't Madhav notice the clash at first?
qa.a: He was so happy and excited after winning that everything felt possible and he didn't see the risks.

qa.q: What did Kishore sir suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He suggested sleeping on it, so Madhav could decide once his joy had settled and see the clashes clearly.

qa.q: How might the classmate who invited Madhav to the hackathon feel if he pulled out?
qa.a: The classmate might feel let down, especially if they had counted on him.

grounding: A young adult in a great mood underestimates risks and says yes to too much.

passage:
Dear Gargi,

Remember when I got that internship offer in May? I was so happy I agreed to everything that week: helping Chachu shift houses, a trip to Rishikesh, and a part-time tutoring job.

I didn't even check dates. Everything felt doable. I thought, I'm on a roll, what could go wrong?

Then all three landed on the same fortnight. I let Chachu down, cancelled the trip, and nearly lost the tutoring job. The internship started and I was already tired.

I'm writing because you've just got your scholarship, and you sound over the moon. Please enjoy it. But before you say yes to anything, sleep on it.

Irfan

qa.q: What three things did Irfan agree to that week?
qa.a: Helping Chachu shift houses, a trip to Rishikesh and a part-time tutoring job.

qa.q: Why did everything feel doable to Irfan in May?
qa.a: Irfan felt joyful and on a roll after the internship offer, so problems seemed unlikely.

qa.q: What advice does Irfan give Gargi, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Sleep on it before saying yes, because a very happy mood can make risks and clashes seem small.

qa.q: How might Chachu have felt when Irfan let him down?
qa.a: Chachu probably felt disappointed and let down, having counted on help with the move.

grounding: A young adult in a great mood says yes to too much, underestimating clashes and risks.

Simran: I'm writing my resignation right now

Simran: I've been thinking about quitting anyway

Simran: saving it as draft

Simran: ya. I'll read it with coffee and see if I still mean it

Simran: read it. deleted it. going to talk to my manager instead 🙂

qa.q: What did Simran save as a draft?
qa.a: The resignation letter.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when first writing the resignation?
qa.a: Simran felt furious about the manager taking credit, and in that anger quitting seemed like the right answer.

qa.q: Why was waiting until the next day a wise choice?
qa.a: Anger makes big choices look urgent, and reading it calmly with coffee let Simran see that quitting wasn't really wanted.

qa.q: How does Deepak help Simran?
qa.a: Deepak stays calm, suggests waiting, and then feels proud when Simran decides to talk instead of quitting.

grounding: A wise person notices anger rising, postpones a big decision, and returns calm to see if the view has changed.

passage:
Rekha had been fighting with her landlord in Nashik for weeks about repairs. One night, after a shouting match on the phone, she opened a flat-listing site and started typing a message: "I'm moving out this month."

Her friend Noor, staying over, saw her face. "You're shaking."

"I'm so angry. I want out."

Noor sat beside her. "You told me last week you love this flat. And moving now would mean breaking the lease."

Rekha stopped typing. She knew this feeling. When she was this angry, every choice looked urgent.

"I'll decide on Sunday," she said, closing the laptop. On Sunday, calmer, she decided to stay and wrote to the landlord asking for the repairs in writing.

qa.q: When did Rekha say she would decide?
qa.a: On Sunday.

qa.q: Why did Rekha stop typing the message?
qa.a: She recognised her anger was making the choice feel urgent, and she felt unsure once Noor reminded her she loved the flat.

qa.q: What did Rekha do differently on Sunday, and why was it better?
qa.a: Calmer, she stayed and asked for repairs in writing, which dealt with the real problem without an angry, rushed move.

qa.q: How might Noor feel watching Rekha close the laptop?
qa.a: Noor probably felt relieved and glad her gentle reminder helped.

grounding: A wise person notices her anger, postpones a big decision and returns calm to see whether her view has changed.

passage:
In Istanbul, Zeynep, twenty-five, received a cold email from her thesis supervisor late one night: "This chapter is not acceptable."

Her first thought was: I'll quit the programme. She even opened a new message to the department.

Then she noticed her hands were trembling and her heart was pounding. She knew she was in no state to decide anything. She texted her sister Rosa instead: "Horrible email. Not replying tonight."

Rosa wrote back: "Smart. Sleep. We'll talk tomorrow."

The next morning, after a walk and breakfast, Zeynep read the email again. It was harsh, but it listed three clear changes. Quitting now seemed absurd. She replied calmly, asking for a meeting.

qa.q: How many changes did the email list?
qa.a: Three clear changes.

qa.q: What was Zeynep feeling when she noticed her hands trembling?
qa.a: She felt distressed and shaken, and knew that in this state she might make a rash choice like quitting.

qa.q: What small step helped Zeynep avoid a hasty decision?
qa.a: Texting Rosa that she wouldn't reply tonight, then rereading the email after a walk and breakfast.

qa.q: What would have changed if Zeynep had replied that night?
qa.a: She might have quit the programme in despair, a choice she found absurd the next morning.

grounding: A wise person notices her distress, postpones a big decision and replies once calm.
